items.prompt: In a rotated ascending array with distinct values, which condition shows that the left half [left, mid] is ordered?

feedback.reason: With distinct values, if the left endpoint is no greater than mid, no rotation pivot lies inside [left, mid].

blocks.text: Use endpoint order to locate the pivot

A single rotation creates one descending break from the former maximum to the former minimum. With distinct values, nums[left] <= nums[mid] means that break is not inside [left, mid], so this inclusive half remains ascending.

items: In [4, 5, 6, 1, 2, 3] with left = 0 and mid = 2, nums[left] = 4 <= 6 = nums[mid].
Values [4, 5, 6] are ascending, while the rotation break lies after mid.
After checking nums[mid] != target, target belongs to this half exactly when nums[left] <= target < nums[mid].

blocks.title: Why distinctness matters
blocks.text: With duplicates, equality can occur on both sides of the pivot and nums[left] == nums[mid] may not reveal which half contains the break.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_le_right: This comparison can certify the right half [mid, right], but it does not establish the requested order of [left, mid].
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_le_mid: Target comparison does not determine whether the half itself is ordered.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_le_right: This may show the whole interval is ordered, but it is not the standard left-half test in the rotated branch.

items.prompt: If nums[left] > nums[mid] in a rotated array with distinct values, what can be concluded?

options.text: The right half [mid, right] is ordered.

feedback.reason: With one rotation and distinct values, the pivot must lie in the left portion when nums[left] > nums[mid].

blocks.text: A descending endpoint comparison places the break on the left
nums[left] > nums[mid] cannot occur inside one ascending segment. Therefore the rotation break lies between left and mid, leaving [mid, right] inside the later ascending segment.

items: In [5, 6, 1, 2, 3, 4], left = 0 and mid = 2 give 5 > 1.
The break 6 -> 1 lies in [left, mid].
The right half [1, 2, 3, 4] is ordered, so its endpoint range can decide whether to retain it.

blocks.title: Structure does not prove existence
blocks.text: Identifying an ordered half says where target could lie based on its value. It does not by itself prove that target occurs anywhere.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_ordered: The strict decrease from nums[left] to nums[mid] proves the rotation break lies inside the left side, so that whole half is not ascending.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_absent: This endpoint comparison reveals the pivot's side but provides no comparison between target and either ordered value range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.array_unsorted: A single rotation breaks global order once but preserves a fully ordered right half in this branch.

items.prompt: The left half is ordered and satisfies nums[left] <= target < nums[mid]. Which side should be retained after nums[mid] is known not to equal target?

options.text: The right side starting at mid + 1.
The left side ending at mid - 1.

feedback.reason: The ordered left half contains every value between its endpoint values exactly once under the distinct-value contract.

blocks.text: Range membership identifies the only possible half

Because [left, mid] is ascending and values are distinct, it contains every array value in its endpoint interval exactly once. The strict target < nums[mid] comparison excludes the midpoint already known not to match.

items: For [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], left = 0 and mid = 3 identify ordered values 4 through 7.
For target 5, 4 <= 5 < 7 places its only possible occurrence in indices 0 through 2.
Set right = mid - 1. Retaining the rotated right half would discard the side whose ordered range contains target.

blocks.title: Endpoint inclusivity
blocks.text: Include nums[left] because left has not been checked separately; exclude nums[mid] only because the exact-match comparison already failed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.right_side: The target lies inside the value range of the ordered left half.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_sides: The ordered-range test provides a legal discard rule.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_mid: The prompt explicitly states nums[mid] is not target, so returning mid would violate the exact-search result contract.

items.prompt: The left half is ordered, but target is smaller than nums[left] or greater than nums[mid]. Which side should be retained?

options.text: The right side starting at mid + 1.

feedback.reason: Range exclusion from the ordered half permits discarding it.

blocks.text: Discard the ordered half only after excluding its value range
When [left, mid] is ordered, every value in that half lies between nums[left] and nums[mid]. If target is below the lower endpoint or above the upper endpoint, it cannot occur there.

items: In [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], the ordered left half spans values 4 through 7.
Target 1 is below 4, so it is outside that half even though 1 < nums[mid].
The rotated right half remains the only possible side; set left = mid + 1.

blocks.title: Classic comparison can point the wrong way
blocks.text: target < nums[mid] would normally search left, but target may be a small post-pivot value on the right. The ordered-half endpoint test supplies the missing context.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.left_side: The target falls outside that half's value range.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_left: Range exclusion says target is not in the ordered half; it does not establish nums[left] == target, so left cannot be returned.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stop: The target may remain in the rotated right half.

items.prompt: How should the algorithm behave when the active interval is not rotated and is fully ascending?

options.text: Return not found because no pivot exists inside the interval.
Switch unconditionally to a full linear scan.
The same ordered-half logic reduces to ordinary binary search.

feedback.reason: An unrotated interval has an ordered left half and an ordered right half.

blocks.text: Zero rotation is part of the same contract

A rotation by zero leaves the entire active interval ascending. The test nums[left] <= nums[mid] identifies the left half as ordered, and the target range selects the same side that ordinary binary search would select.

items: For [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], mid value 5 splits two ordered halves.
Target 3 lies in [nums[left], nums[mid]), so the algorithm moves right to mid - 1.
Target 7 lies outside that left range, so it moves left to mid + 1.

blocks.title: No special pivot branch is needed
blocks.text: The local-order proof covers both rotated and unrotated active intervals. Absence of a pivot inside the interval is not a failure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.fail_rotation: Zero rotation is a valid case under the rotated-array contract, and the fully ascending interval retains all binary-search structure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_only: Both halves are ordered, so endpoint range comparisons still discard about half; an unconditional scan throws away valid logarithmic structure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reverse: Reversing an ascending interval would make it descending and mutate input without helping the ordered-half proof.

items.prompt: A one-element rotated array contains target. What should happen?

options.text: The loop should skip because no half can be identified.
Both boundaries should move before comparison.
The midpoint is index 0 and should be returned.

feedback.reason: Rotated search retains the exact-match check before structural half classification.

blocks.text: A singleton must be compared before any discard
With left = right = 0, the closed active interval contains one candidate and mid = 0. The first action in the iteration is the exact comparison nums[mid] == target.

items: The loop condition left <= right admits the singleton.
mid = 0 is a valid index and its value equals target by the premise.
Return 0 immediately; ordered-half classification is needed only after a mismatch.

blocks.title: Why order matters
blocks.text: Moving boundaries before the exact check would discard the only candidate and turn a present target into a false not-found result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_singleton: A closed singleton interval contains one unchecked candidate, and skipping it can miss the target at index 0.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_not_found: Rotation has no adverse effect on one value; the premise says that sole value equals target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.move_both: Moving boundaries before comparison discards the only possible index and converts a present target into a false miss.

items.prompt: Why is comparing target only with nums[mid] insufficient after a mismatch in a rotated array?

options.text: nums[mid] cannot be read after rotation.
The global order is broken at the pivot, so direction requires identifying an ordered half and checking its endpoint range.
Targets in rotated arrays are never numeric.

feedback.reason: A simple target < nums[mid] comparison may point across the rotation pivot incorrectly.

blocks.text: The pivot breaks the global comparison implication
Ordinary binary search uses target < nums[mid] to infer that target, if present, is left. In a rotated array, small values may lie after the pivot on the right, so that implication is false globally.

items: In [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], mid contains 7 and target 0 is smaller.
Searching left from that comparison alone would discard target at index 4.
Identify [4, 5, 6, 7] as the ordered half, observe 0 is outside its endpoint range, and retain the right side.

blocks.title: Local order restores elimination
blocks.text: At least one half is ascending under the distinct-value contract. Its endpoint range—not the midpoint comparison alone—proves which side cannot contain target.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_unreadable: Rotation changes value order but not index validity, so nums[mid] remains readable inside the active interval.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_not_numeric: The same pivot and endpoint-range reasoning works for any distinct values under a consistent total order, not only numbers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_halves_unsorted: At least one half is ordered under the distinct-value contract.

items.prompt: What problem do equal values create when nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right]?

options.text: The input can no longer be considered rotated.
The comparisons may not reveal which half contains the rotation pivot.

feedback.reason: Distinct-value reasoning relies on a strict structural comparison.

blocks.text: Equality can hide the pivot

When nums[left], nums[mid], and nums[right] are equal, endpoint comparisons fit both a pivot-free interval and an interval whose pivot is hidden among equal values. Neither half is uniquely certified by those values.

items: In [1, 0, 1, 1, 1], left, mid, and right can all hold 1 while target 0 lies across the hidden break.
After confirming the equal value is not target, equal endpoints can be removed without losing a matching endpoint.
This may expose structure, but it guarantees only constant boundary shrink rather than half elimination.

blocks.title: Duplicate contract changes complexity
blocks.text: Boundary shrinking preserves correctness, but arbitrary duplicate runs can force repeated ambiguous iterations and linear worst-case time.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_found: The equal endpoint value may differ from target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.array_invalid: Rotated arrays may contain duplicates under a broader contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_overflow: Equality among stored values says nothing about whether left + (right - left) / 2 overflows; the defect is structural ambiguity.

items.prompt: When duplicate ambiguity is resolved by incrementing left and decrementing right, what worst-case behavior becomes possible?

feedback.reason: Repeated equal endpoints can force the algorithm to discard only one or two positions per iteration.

blocks.text: Measure progress on an all-equal interval
If every active value is the same non-target value, nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right] holds on every iteration. Structural comparisons cannot select a half.

items: Incrementing left and decrementing right removes at most two candidates.
Starting with n candidates can therefore require about n / 2 ambiguous iterations.
That is Θ(n) worst-case work even though non-ambiguous iterations still halve the interval.

blocks.title: Correctness and speed separate
blocks.text: Removing endpoints known not to equal target is safe. The lost guarantee is logarithmic progress, not correctness.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: On an all-equal absent-target input, ambiguity persists and the algorithm may remove endpoints through the entire array.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.log_squared: The interval may shrink by one rather than by half.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.factorial: Each iteration follows one branch and removes candidates; it never enumerates permutations or creates factorial branching.

items.prompt: An ascending array is rotated by one position so the former last element moves to index 0. Which edge case does this test?

options.text: The rotation pivot lies immediately after the first element.

feedback.reason: Rotations near either boundary test whether ordered-half detection works when one sorted region is very small.

blocks.text: Locate the descending break
Rotating ascending [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] right by one position produces [5, 1, 2, 3, 4]. The unique descending break is 5 -> 1.

items: The former maximum occupies index 0.
The smallest element—the rotation pivot under the common definition—occupies index 1, immediately after the first element.
This leaves a one-element high-value segment and a long ordered low-value segment, stressing a pivot near the left edge.

blocks.title: Test both directions
blocks.text: Also rotate left by one so the pivot lies near the other edge. The algorithm must not assume balanced sorted regions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_rotation: Moving the last element to the front changes the pivot.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_duplicates: Rotation only repositions the existing distinct values and cannot create extra copies of them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.descending_order: The result [last, first, ..., penultimate] has one descending break, while the long suffix remains ascending.

items.prompt: The left half [left, mid] is ordered. Which conditions place target inside that half? Select all that apply.

options.text: target equals nums[mid], before the mismatch branch is entered.

feedback.reason: The ordered half covers its inclusive endpoint-value range under distinct values.

blocks.text: Separate full-half membership from the mismatch branch
The ordered inclusive half [left, mid] contains values from nums[left] through nums[mid]. Therefore equality at either endpoint and every strict interior value place target in that half.

items: target == nums[left] is inside because left is included.
nums[left] < target < nums[mid] is strictly inside the ordered value interval.
target == nums[mid] is also inside and should be returned by the exact-match check before any mismatch branch.
Only after nums[mid] != target is known does the branch use the strict upper test target < nums[mid].

blocks.title: Value range follows index range
blocks.text: Because the half is ascending with distinct values, its inclusive index endpoints define its inclusive value range.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.greater_mid: Every value in the ordered left half is <= nums[mid], so a strictly greater target cannot occur there.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.at_left: The index interval includes left, and its value equals target under this condition.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.strict_inside: Ascending order places a target strictly between the endpoint values inside this half's value range.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.at_mid: Mid belongs to [left, mid], and the algorithm should return it before entering mismatch-only range logic.

items.prompt: Which test cases are important for rotated-array search? Select all that apply.

options.text: Only one case where target begins at the first midpoint.
Pivot near the first or last position.

feedback.reason: Rotated search needs structural edge cases, not just a midpoint equality case.

blocks.text: Exercise every structural branch
An immediate midpoint hit bypasses ordered-half detection and both boundary updates. A useful test set must force the pivot and target onto different sides and must reach minimal intervals.

items: No rotation verifies the generalized logic reduces to classic binary search.
A pivot near either edge stresses one very short and one long ordered region.
Singleton hit and miss verify exact-check order, loop equality, and not-found exit.
For each shape, include targets in each region and an absent target.

blocks.title: Duplicates require a separate matrix
blocks.text: If the contract permits duplicates, also test equal endpoints hiding the pivot and verify the documented linear worst case.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.only_middle_hit: Returning on the first comparison does not execute ordered-half detection, range exclusion, endpoint convergence, or an absent-target path.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.no_rotation: Zero rotation must choose the same legal side as classic binary search rather than treating the missing pivot as failure.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.pivot_edges: These shapes prove half detection does not assume the descending break lies near mid.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.singleton_absent: Hit and miss cases test the final candidate and the empty-interval not-found transition.

items.prompt: Which statements are correct when duplicates are allowed? Select all that apply.

options.text: Equal endpoint and midpoint values can make the ordered half ambiguous.
The search is always O(log n) despite arbitrary duplicates.
Worst-case time may degrade to O(n).
A correct strategy may shrink equal boundaries before continuing.

feedback.reason: Duplicates weaken the structural information used for half elimination.

blocks.text: Equal values preserve candidates but hide structure
When nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right] and the shared value is not target, those endpoints are safe to remove. Their equality, however, does not reveal which side contains the rotation break.

items: Check mid first; if it matched, return immediately.
When all three values are the same non-target, increment left and decrement right.
Repeat structural analysis on the preserved interior.
An all-equal absent-target input can repeat this O(n) times.

blocks.title: The distinct-value theorem no longer applies
blocks.text: Do not claim one half is identifiable from a non-strict comparison when equal values can straddle the pivot.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_log: An all-equal absent-target interval may shrink by only its endpoints each iteration, producing linear rather than logarithmic progress.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.ordered_half_ambiguous: Equal endpoint and midpoint values are compatible with the pivot lying on either side, so the comparison does not localize it.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.shrink_boundaries: After equality to the nonmatching midpoint proves both endpoints are not target, removing them preserves every possible occurrence.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.worst_linear: If ambiguity persists, discarding only one or two values per iteration takes a linear number of iterations.

items.prompt: Arrange one distinct-value rotated-array search iteration.

elements.text: Determine whether the left or right half is ordered.
Check whether target lies inside the ordered half's endpoint range.
Retain that half if target is inside; otherwise retain the other half.

feedback.reason: Exact match is resolved first, then local order supports a range-based discard decision.

blocks.text: Each decision depends on the previous one

The array is globally broken at one pivot, so a mismatch cannot use classic direction immediately. Distinctness guarantees a locally ordered half whose endpoint range restores a safe elimination proof.
Iteration order

items: Compare nums[mid] with target and return before excluding mid if they are equal.
On mismatch, compare nums[left] with nums[mid] to determine whether [left, mid] is ordered; otherwise [mid, right] is ordered.
Compare target with the ordered half's endpoint values, excluding mid only because it already mismatched.
Retain the ordered half when target lies in its range; otherwise retain the other half, removing mid with a plus-or-minus-one update.

blocks.title: Invariant
blocks.text: If target exists, its unique index remains inside [left, right]. Every mismatch branch must prove the discarded side cannot contain it.

items.prompt: When the left half is ordered and mid is not target, which branch rules are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: If target is inside the ordered left range, set left = mid + 1.
If target is inside, set right = mid - 1.

feedback.reason: The ordered-half endpoint range determines whether it can contain target.

blocks.text: Four independent branch facts
After nums[mid] != target, nums[left] <= nums[mid] certifies an ascending left half. Its remaining possible target range is nums[left] <= target < nums[mid].

items: Confirm left order before using endpoint range membership.
Include nums[left], whose index remains unchecked; exclude nums[mid], whose mismatch is known.
If target is inside, right = mid - 1 retains the only possible side.
If target is outside, left = mid + 1 discards the ordered half and retains the pivot-containing side.

blocks.title: Wrong-way counterexample
blocks.text: For [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] and target 5, moving left after detecting target inside [4, 7) would discard the actual index 1.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.inside_move_left: When target lies inside the ordered left range, moving left to mid + 1 discards the only half whose value interval can contain target.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.confirm_left_order: Endpoint range reasoning is sound only after nums[left] <= nums[mid] certifies that no pivot break lies in the left half.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.check_range: The inclusive lower and strict upper comparisons match unchecked left and already-rejected mid.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.inside_move_right: Range membership places any unique occurrence before mid, so right must move to mid - 1.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.outside_move_left: Range exclusion proves the ordered left half cannot contain target, so the other side is retained with left = mid + 1.

items.prompt: Arrange a duplicate-ambiguity branch when nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right] and mid is not target.

elements.text: Recognize that neither half can be proven ordered from the equality.
Increment left and decrement right after confirming those endpoint values are not target.
Repeat structural analysis on the smaller interval.

feedback.reason: Equal nonmatching endpoints can be removed without losing target, but only limited progress is guaranteed.

blocks.text: Remove only values proved not to be target

The premise gives nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right] and nums[mid] != target. Equality therefore proves both endpoint values also differ from target, even though it reveals nothing about the pivot's side.
Ambiguity branch

items: Recognize that equal boundary comparisons cannot certify which half contains the descending break.
Use equality to the nonmatching midpoint to prove indices left and right are not target, then increment left and decrement right.
Preserve every interior index because target may still occur on either side of the hidden pivot.
Repeat exact-match and structural analysis on the smaller interval.

blocks.title: Progress guarantee
blocks.text: This branch removes endpoints but may not halve the interval. A long duplicate run therefore permits Θ(n) worst-case iterations.

items.prompt: A rotated sorted array contains n distinct values, and each mismatch discards about half of the active interval. Select worst-case time and iterative auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Distinct values guarantee enough structural information to choose one side each iteration.

blocks.text: Half elimination preserves logarithmic search

After an exact mismatch, distinct endpoint comparisons identify an ordered half. Target range membership proves one half impossible, and the premise says the update leaves at most about half the active candidates.
Time and space derivation

items: After k mismatches, at most about n / 2^k candidates remain.
Reaching an empty or singleton interval takes O(log n) iterations, including the absent-target worst case.
Each iteration performs O(1) comparisons and arithmetic, so time is O(log n).
The iterative implementation stores only left, right, mid, and constant comparison state, so auxiliary space is O(1).

blocks.title: Distinctness is a complexity premise
blocks.text: It guarantees structural half selection. Removing it without another rule invalidates the logarithmic worst-case claim.

items.prompt: A rotated sorted array may contain arbitrary duplicates, and equal endpoints are removed one step at a time when structure is ambiguous. Select worst-case time and iterative auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Duplicate ambiguity can prevent half elimination and force linear boundary shrinking.

blocks.text: An all-equal counterexample sets the worst case
Consider n copies of value 1 and an absent target 2. Every midpoint and both endpoints are equal, so no iteration can identify a structural half from values.
Worst-case accounting

items: The ambiguity branch removes one or two endpoints, so Θ(n) candidates may be inspected before absence is proven.
Non-ambiguous inputs can still finish in O(log n), but worst-case time is O(n).
No candidates are copied; the algorithm retains a constant number of boundary and comparison variables.
Iterative auxiliary space is therefore O(1).

blocks.title: Worst case versus typical case
blocks.text: Occasional duplicate ambiguity does not force every input to be linear. The all-equal family proves only that logarithmic time cannot be guaranteed.
